newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - US housing starts seen tempered in March.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US housing starts seen tempered in March.

text.p: The pace of U.S. housing starts probably slowed modestly in March after roaring ahead in February at its fastest clip in nearly three years, economists said on Monday.
Experts said February's extraordinary gains were related to the weather and the expected pull back in March should not be interpreted as a crack in the robust new-homes market.
A Reuters poll of economists called for a 4.45 percent decline in March housing starts to 1.46 million units on an annualized basis from 1.528 million units in February.
The Commerce Department will release its housing starts report at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Wednesday.
Despite a continued boom in U.S. consumer spending, tight labor markets, and shrinking new home inventories, most economists said February's growth surge would not be repeated in March.

"The levels we reached in the prior month are unsustainable," said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp, who expected new home sales to annualize 1.48 million units in March.
But a handful of experts said February's strength could not be "explained away" by early spring-like weather and they forecast a rise in March.

"We think the momentum is still up in that sector and we're looking to see some modest increases built on top of what we have seen already this year," said Robert Brusca, chief economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc, who predicted a rise to 1.55 million units in March.
Economists were unanimous that a recent back-up in U.S. interest rates would not affect the March or even April data.
With the growing popularity of adjustable rate mortgages, economists said potential home owners may be less adverse to higher rates now than ever before.
"Due to adjustable rate mortgages, higher rates will be slow to have an impact. We will see stabilization, but the higher rates won't take affect probably until quarters ahead," DLJ's Schaja said.
Analysts also said in the short-run, prospects for higher rates can spark a bout of home buying.
"The home sales data may pick-up (in future months) because of the recent back-up in rates," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc.

"It imposes what you could call panic buying on the part of people who have been scratching around on whether they should do it now or later," he added. Karydakis predicted a 1.45 million units reading for March.
